Preparation of Carbon Electrode Material with a Large
Speciﬁc Surface Area and Multiscale Pore Structure from
Biowaste Kochia for Symmetrical Supercapacitor
Kai Fan, Xiping Lei,* Junzhan Zhang,* Ting Yu, Haonan Chen, and Jing Liu
1. Introduction
Recently, the excessive consumption of fossil fuel energy and the
deterioration of the living environment have attracted strong
attention, prompting the scientiﬁc community to turn to research
on renewable green energy such as wind energy, solar energy,
and hydropower, but they all have a common shortcoming that
is intermittent and dif ﬁcult to satisfy today ’s world with increas-
ing demand for energy. [1–3] And with the continuous expansion
of the electric vehicle market, people have increased the demand
for environmentally friendly, renewable resources with the high
power density and high energy density. [4,5] Therefore, to solve
this problem, it is necessary to study sustainable energy produc-
tion and storage technology.
Among various energy storage devices, supercapacitors, as a
very ideal energy storage device have a higher power density than
batteries,[6] a higher energy density than
traditional capacitors, [7] fast charging
speed,[8] and excellent cycle performance, [9]
have been studied. Among them, electrode
materials play a vital role in the capacitance
performance of supercapacitors. Electrode
materials that are currently being studied
extensively include carbon materials, con-
ductive polymers, and metal oxides. [10–12]
Carbon-based materials with electric
double-layer capacitance behavior, such
as activated carbon, have a rich pore struc-
ture, large speci ﬁc surface, and good cycle
stability.[13–15] They have the conditions for
the preparation of excellent electrode mate-
rials and have attracted attention. However,
traditional activated carbon is produced
from coal and its derivatives, which is
non-renewable and its high cost limits its
development. In contrast, to comply with
the global advocacy of the circular economy
and the effective reuse of resources, waste
biomass can be used as the main raw mate-
rial for the preparation of activated carbon. [2] Among them,
plants with high carbon content, speci ﬁc structure and composi-
tion, and renewable nature can be the preferred biomass carbon
source. Through the high-temperature carbonization process,
the lignocellulose in the original plant skeleton is removed to
form a carbon skeleton and a porous structure.[16] However, most
plant-based carbon materials have the disadvantages of low spe-
ciﬁc capacitance, inconspicuous pore structure, and small spe-
ciﬁc surface area (SSA) through simple high-temperature
pyrolysis.[17] Activators such as potassium hydroxide, [18] sodium
hydroxide,[19] and phosphoric acid [20] have been studied to opti-
mize them. The use of chemical activators can ameliorate the
porous structure of different morphologies and optimize the
SSA.[21–23] The improved pore structure will signi ﬁcantly accel-
erate the transport rate of electrolyte ions and have more active
sites. Some studies have developed activated carbon for superca-
pacitor electrode materials by directly carbonizing waste plants.
Yifu Zhang prepared biomass activated carbon by directly car-
bonizing kelp, bamboo leaves, and waste rice husks, not only
achieved waste recycling and reuse to prepare new energy carbon
materials with excellent pore structure but also used carbon
materials with excellent pore structure as a substrate to prepare
composite materials with higher speciﬁc capacitance.[24–27] Other
studies have used a combination of carbonization and KOH acti-
vation, such as Zhanglin Liu used lignocellulose-rich waste

Kochia that is used as Chinese herbal medicine is always abandoned as a
biowaste after extracting useful components. However, the richness of ligno-
cellulose and the natural tubular structure make it a potential source of biomass
carbon. After high-temperature pyrolysis at 800 °C and further etching by proper
activation conditions, a graded porous structured carbon-based supercapacitor
electrode material (KAC-5) can be obtained. The electrode material is prepared in
a 1:5 carbon-to-base ratio, possessing a speci ﬁc surface area of 1441.30 m 2 g/C0 1,
and a graded macro-meso-micro structure that is rich in micropores. The
capacitance retention retains at 90.31% even after 10 000 cycles in 6 M KOH
electrolyte and exhibits outstanding capacitance performance with a speci ﬁc
capacitance of 284 F g /C0 1 at a current density of 1 A g /C0 1. The symmetrical
supercapacitor is assembled with KAC-5 and also has good cycling stability in 6 M
KOH aqueous electrolyte, reaching 88.83% after 10 000 cycles with an energy
density of 12.3 Wh kg /C0 1 at a power density of 300 W kg /C0 1. Based on the above,
sustainable preparation of energy storage material from waste biomass for high
capacitance and stable biomass-based supercapacitors has been achieved.

Tailoring Porosity and Surface Functionality in Activated 
Carbon via Synergistic Ultrasonic and Microwave Activation 
for Energy Storage Applications 
Ayten Ateş1 Zaid Rossi2 
1 Faculty of Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Sivas Cumhuriyet University, Sivas, Türkiye 2 Materials, Systems and Energy Engineering 
Laboratory (MaSEEL) -UAE/U04FSTTg- Faculty of Sciences and Techniques of Tangier, Abdelmalek Essaâdi University, Tétouan, Morocco 
Correspondence: Ayten Ateş( ates@cumhuriyet.edu.tr) 
Received: 8 November 2025 Revised: 12 January 2026 Accepted: 16 February 2026 
Keywords: acid activation | activated carbon | hazelnut shell | supercapacitor | ultrasonic activation 
ABSTRACT 
Hazelnut shell–derived activated carbons were synthesized via phosphoric acid chemical activation and subsequently modified 
using microwave (MW) and ultrasonic (US) treatments to tailor their physicochemical and electrochemical properties for 
supercapacitor applications. Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirmed the formation of turbostratic carbon frameworks 
with partial graphitic ordering and abundant surface functional groups. Elemental analysis revealed that microwave treatment 
induced pronounced surface oxidation, whereas ultrasonic treatment preserved high carbon content while introducing moderate 
oxygen functionalities. Thermal analysis demonstrated superior thermal stability for the ultrasound-assisted activated carbon. 
Electrochemical performance was evaluated in a three-electrode system using 3 M KOH electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry revealed 
dominant electrical double-layer capacitive behavior with minor pseudocapacitive contributions, particularly for the ultrasound- 
treated sample. Among all electrodes, ACA-US exhibited the largest CV area, highest current response, and superior specific 
capacitance, attributed to its exceptionally high BET surface area (2138 m2 g− 1 ) and well-developed microporosity. Galvanostatic 
charge–discharge measurements confirmed excellent reversibility and rate capability, with ACA-US delivering the longest 
discharge times and highest capacitance over a wide current density range. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy revealed 
reduced charge transfer resistance and improved ion diffusion kinetics for ACA-US. Furthermore, the optimized electrode 
retained ∼ 85% of its initial capacitance after 2000 cycles, indicating excellent long-term stability. These results demonstrate that 
ultrasonic post-treatment is an effective strategy for producing high-performance biomass-derived activated carbons for advanced 
supercapacitor applications.

ABSTRACT: The production of value-added materials from waste
resources is a sustainable approach for solid waste management. Facile
yet economic conversion of carbon-neutral biowastes into a metal-free
porous carbon material with a high oxygen reduction reaction (ORR)
and capacitive energy storage efficiency is critical for renewable energy
conversion and storage technologies. Herein, a microporous carbon
with a self-doped N heteroatom (ALPC) was successfully prepared
from waste agarwood leaves through a chemical activation process.
The synthesized ALPC-800 material containing N (11.23 atom %)
and O (8.54 atom %) with a high surface area as an electrocatalyst for
ORR shows an onset potential (E
onset
) of 0.98 V and excellent limiting
current density (J
L
) of 6.09 mA cm
−2
, which are comparable to 10 wt % Pt/C. ALPC-800 as an electrocatalyst shows a four-electron
transfer-mediated ORR process which is supported by both experimental and theoretical findings. Also, ALPC-800 in a three-
electrode configuration for supercapacitors presented a high specific capacitance of 421 F g
−1
at a current density of 1 A g
−1
in an
acidic electrolyte. More prominently, the assembled symmetrical supercapacitor device based on ALPC-800 demonstrated a high
capacitance retention of 91% after 6000 cycles at 1 A g
−1
with a remarkable energy density of 21.15 Wh kg
−1
and a power density of
4.93 kW kg
−1
. Thus, this work provides an environmentally benign, simple, efficient, and economical method for energy storage and
conversion applications. Being a metal-free catalyst, heteroatom-doped ALPC-800 carbon material synthesized from biowaste has the
potential to replace the commercially available high-cost Pt/C catalyst for fuel cell application.
KEYWORDS: waste leaves, N-doped graphitic carbon, metal-free ORR, supercapacitor, clean energy conversion

INTRODUCTION
In the past few decades, with the ever-increasing depletion of
fossil fuel reserves and rising environmental pollution,
extensive research efforts have been dedicated for the
technological advancement of sustainable energy storage and
conversion systems.
1−3
Within the context of fossil-free and
efficient energy applications, the oxygen reduction reaction
(ORR) and supercapacitors have been enormously inves-
tigated, and yet, the fundamental challenge remains in the
design and development of highly efficient, low-cost electro-
active materials.
4
In fuel cells, ORR is an important
electrochemical reaction which takes place at the cathodic
site.
5,6
Pt-based electrocatalysts are generally recognized to
deliver excellent ORR activities due to their high current
density and remarkable electrochemical kinetic process.
7
However, high cost, scarcity, substandard durability, and
susceptibility to methanol tolerance are the major inherent
hurdles for bulk-scale commercial application.
8,9
Though
transition metal-based electrocatalysts have become alterna-
tives to Pt/C for boosting the performance of the ORR
process,
10,11
critical issues still remain in terms of their poor
chemical stability, irregular distribution of active sites, high
price, and eco-unfriendliness. In this regard, carbon-based
nanomaterials like graphene and carbon nanotubes have been
widely explored as electrode materials for ORR on account of
their robust stability, high electrical conductivity, and large
surface area.
12−14
Despite their excellent performances, wide-
reaching utilizations for practical application are strictly
controlled by the high cost, low yield, and complex synthetic
conditions.
